passages.title: The lovers speak and exchange praise
passages.summary: The book is called the Song of songs. A woman speaks first and longs for her lover’s kisses. She says his love is better than wine and his name is like perfume. She tells the women of Jerusalem that she is dark and lovely. The sun has darkened her, since her brothers made her tend the vineyards. She asks her lover where he pastures his flock. He praises her beauty and compares her to a fine mare. She says he is like a bundle of myrrh and a cluster of henna.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: The Church’s Bible Dictionary reports the JST: “the Songs of Solomon are not inspired writings.” How does the woman answer those who stare at her skin?

contextNote.title: Scent brings the lover into the poem
contextNote.text: The woman’s voice opens the book, and she speaks more than anyone in it. Verse 3 begins with scent. His oils are fragrant, and his name is like oil poured out. A good name spreads as perfume does. The comparison makes attraction felt through the senses. Read these images as poetic comparisons, not a list of objects owned by the lovers. Ancient perfume vessels help make that sensory world concrete.

passages.title: Spring brings an invitation
passages.summary: The woman calls herself a flower of the plain. Her lover says she is a lily among thorns. She says he is an apple tree among the trees of the forest. She asks the women of Jerusalem not to stir up love before its time. She hears him coming, leaping over the hills. He looks through the window and calls her to come away. Winter is past, the flowers appear, and the doves are heard. She says her beloved is hers and she is his.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: Why does the woman place a warning about love beside spring’s invitation?

contextNote.title: Seasonal change becomes an invitation
contextNote.text: The lover’s invitation rests on the season. Verse 11 says the winter and the rain are over. Verses 12–13 add flowers, birdsong, figs, and blossoming vines. Everything is ready, so he says, “Arise.” Verse 7 warned not to wake love until it pleases. The two fit together. Love has a right time, as the spring does.

passages.title: A night search and a royal carriage
passages.summary: At night on her bed the woman looks for the one she loves. She does not find him. She gets up and searches the streets and squares. The watchmen find her, and she asks whether they have seen him. Just past them she finds him and holds him. She will not let go until she brings him to her mother’s house. Then a grand procession comes up from the wilderness. It is Solomon’s carriage, guarded by sixty armed men.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: How does the woman’s night search differ from Solomon’s guarded procession?

contextNote.title: Searching gives desire movement
contextNote.text: The phrase “him whom my soul loves” comes four times in verses 1–4. The word “sought” comes four times as well. The scene begins on her bed at night, so it may be a dream. In verse 2 she acts: she gets up and goes through the city. She searches in public and asks the guards. Verse 4 ends with finding and holding. The royal carriage in verses 7–8 needs sixty swords against the night.

passages.title: Praise through animals, towers, and gardens
passages.summary: The man praises the woman’s beauty part by part. Her eyes are doves, and her hair is like goats on a hillside. Her neck is like a tower hung with shields. One glance from her has captured his heart. Her love is better than wine, and her lips drip honey. He calls her a locked garden and a sealed spring. The garden holds pomegranates, nard, saffron, cinnamon, and myrrh. She calls the winds to blow and invites him into the garden.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: What does the woman’s garden invitation add to the lover’s praise?

contextNote.title: The garden describes desire through a place
contextNote.text: Verse 12 calls the woman a locked garden and a sealed fountain. The garden is hers, and it is not open to the public. Verses 13–14 fill it with rare spices and fruit. The picture is of great worth kept private. Verse 16 gives the key to her. She calls the winds and invites him in. “My garden” becomes “his garden” by her own word.

passages.title: A missed visit and a harmful search
passages.summary: The man says he has come into his garden. Then the woman tells of a night when her heart was awake. Her beloved knocked and asked her to open. She had undressed and washed her feet, and she hesitated. When she opened the door, he was gone. She searched and called, and he did not answer. The watchmen found her, beat her, and took her cloak. The women ask what makes him special, and she describes him from head to foot.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: How do the watchmen’s actions change the woman’s search from chapter 3?

contextNote.title: A missed opening changes the scene
contextNote.text: In verse 3 the woman gives small reasons for not getting up. By verse 6 she has opened the door, and he has left. The moment was missed. Her search repeats chapter 3 with a different result. There the watchmen let her pass (3:3). Here they strike and wound her (verse 7). The poem lets love include bad timing and hurt.

passages.title: The women offer help
passages.summary: The women of Jerusalem ask where her beloved has gone. They offer to look for him with her. She answers that he has gone down to his garden. She says she is his and he is hers. He praises her as beautiful as a great city and awesome as an army. Her eyes overwhelm him. A king may have many queens, but she is his only one. She went down to the orchard to see whether the vines had budded.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: How does the women’s offer answer the request she made in chapter 5?

contextNote.title: Belonging follows a question about absence
contextNote.text: In 2:16 the woman said, “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” Verse 3 reverses the order. Now she says first, “I am my beloved’s.” This comes after the lost night of chapter 5. She states their belonging again and names where he is (verse 2). Verses 8–9 set her apart from a king’s many wives. Verse 9 calls her “unique.”

passages.title: The woman invites her lover outside
passages.summary: The man praises the woman from her feet to her head. Her neck is like an ivory tower, and her eyes are like pools. Her hair holds a king captive. She is like a palm tree, and he will climb it. She says she belongs to her beloved and his desire is for her. She invites him to go out to the fields and stay in the villages. They will rise early to see whether the vines have budded. There she will give him her love.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: How does the woman take action after hearing the lover’s praise?

contextNote.title: Praise leads into the woman’s invitation
contextNote.text: Verse 10 gives a third form of the belonging line. She is his, and “his desire is toward me.” Genesis 3:16 used “desire” in a sentence about strain between husband and wife. Here the desire is mutual and glad. In verses 11–12 she makes the plan. She says, “Let’s go,” “let’s lodge,” and “let’s see.” The praise she has received leads to her own invitation.

passages.title: Love, family control, and a woman’s answer
passages.summary: The woman wishes she could kiss her lover in public without scorn. She asks again that love not be stirred before its time. She asks him to set her as a seal on his heart and arm. Love is as strong as death, and its flame is a mighty fire. Her brothers discuss how to guard their little sister. She answers that she is a wall and has found peace. Solomon rents out a vineyard for silver, but her vineyard is her own. She calls her beloved to hurry like a gazelle.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: How does the woman’s answer differ from her brothers’ plans for her?

contextNote.title: The ending places love beyond purchase
contextNote.text: Verses 6–7 are the one place this book speaks about love in general. Many waters cannot put it out. A man who offered all his wealth for it would be scorned. Love cannot be drowned, and it cannot be bought. Two scenes then test that claim. Her brothers plan to guard her, and she says she guards herself (verses 8–10). Solomon’s vineyard earns silver, and hers is not for rent (verses 11–12).

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

guides.title: Song of Solomon: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Scent brings the lover into the poem
steps.text: The woman’s voice opens the book, and she speaks more than anyone in it. Verse 3 begins with scent. His oils are fragrant, and his name is like oil poured out. A good name spreads as perfume does. The comparison makes attraction felt through the senses. Read these images as poetic comparisons, not a list of objects owned by the lovers. Ancient perfume vessels help make that sensory world concrete.

steps.title: The garden describes desire through a place
steps.text: Verse 12 calls the woman a locked garden and a sealed fountain. The garden is hers, and it is not open to the public. Verses 13–14 fill it with rare spices and fruit. The picture is of great worth kept private. Verse 16 gives the key to her. She calls the winds and invites him in. “My garden” becomes “his garden” by her own word.

steps.title: The ending places love beyond purchase
steps.text: Verses 6–7 are the one place this book speaks about love in general. Many waters cannot put it out. A man who offered all his wealth for it would be scorned. Love cannot be drowned, and it cannot be bought. Two scenes then test that claim. Her brothers plan to guard her, and she says she guards herself (verses 8–10). Solomon’s vineyard earns silver, and hers is not for rent (verses 11–12).

chapterMaps.narrative: The book is called the Song of songs. A woman speaks first and longs for her lover’s kisses. She says his love is better than wine and his name is like perfume. She tells the women of Jerusalem that she is dark and lovely. The sun has darkened her, since her brothers made her tend the vineyards. She asks her lover where he pastures his flock. He praises her beauty and compares her to a fine mare. She says he is like a bundle of myrrh and a cluster of henna.

chapterMaps.narrative: The woman calls herself a flower of the plain. Her lover says she is a lily among thorns. She says he is an apple tree among the trees of the forest. She asks the women of Jerusalem not to stir up love before its time. She hears him coming, leaping over the hills. He looks through the window and calls her to come away. Winter is past, the flowers appear, and the doves are heard. She says her beloved is hers and she is his.

chapterMaps.narrative: At night on her bed the woman looks for the one she loves. She does not find him. She gets up and searches the streets and squares. The watchmen find her, and she asks whether they have seen him. Just past them she finds him and holds him. She will not let go until she brings him to her mother’s house. Then a grand procession comes up from the wilderness. It is Solomon’s carriage, guarded by sixty armed men.

chapterMaps.narrative: The man praises the woman’s beauty part by part. Her eyes are doves, and her hair is like goats on a hillside. Her neck is like a tower hung with shields. One glance from her has captured his heart. Her love is better than wine, and her lips drip honey. He calls her a locked garden and a sealed spring. The garden holds pomegranates, nard, saffron, cinnamon, and myrrh. She calls the winds to blow and invites him into the garden.

chapterMaps.narrative: The man says he has come into his garden. Then the woman tells of a night when her heart was awake. Her beloved knocked and asked her to open. She had undressed and washed her feet, and she hesitated. When she opened the door, he was gone. She searched and called, and he did not answer. The watchmen found her, beat her, and took her cloak. The women ask what makes him special, and she describes him from head to foot.

chapterMaps.narrative: The women of Jerusalem ask where her beloved has gone. They offer to look for him with her. She answers that he has gone down to his garden. She says she is his and he is hers. He praises her as beautiful as a great city and awesome as an army. Her eyes overwhelm him. A king may have many queens, but she is his only one. She went down to the orchard to see whether the vines had budded.

chapterMaps.narrative: The man praises the woman from her feet to her head. Her neck is like an ivory tower, and her eyes are like pools. Her hair holds a king captive. She is like a palm tree, and he will climb it. She says she belongs to her beloved and his desire is for her. She invites him to go out to the fields and stay in the villages. They will rise early to see whether the vines have budded. There she will give him her love.

chapterMaps.narrative: The woman wishes she could kiss her lover in public without scorn. She asks again that love not be stirred before its time. She asks him to set her as a seal on his heart and arm. Love is as strong as death, and its flame is a mighty fire. Her brothers discuss how to guard their little sister. She answers that she is a wall and has found peace. Solomon rents out a vineyard for silver, but her vineyard is her own. She calls her beloved to hurry like a gazelle.
